results.seed: What are datasets for scientific fact verification?

harder.updated_question: What are datasets for scientific fact verification?
harder.verification_criterion: The answer includes at least one publicly available dataset specifically designed for scientific fact verification, with its correct name.

attempts.answer:
Below is a concise map of publicly available datasets used for scientific fact verification, grouped by problem setting and coverage. For each category, we highlight representative datasets, how claims and evidence are sourced, typical tasks, and known limitations or strengths. Where available, we report size/coverage and evaluation metrics.

Quick orientation
- Text-only claim verification over scientific literature: SciFact, COVID-Fact, HealthVer, ClimateFEVER, PubHealth, and their successors/variants.
- Literature-grounded biomedical QA: PubMedQA, MEDQA, QMSum/LSHTA (for summarization-driven verification).
- Structured/visual evidence: tabular (TabFact, FEVEROUS) and chart-based (ClimateViz) verification requiring numerical/statistical reasoning.
- Large-scale/LLM-era science claim corpora: NSF-SciFy (grant proposals), SciClaimHunt (and numeric variant), Multi2Claim (MCQ-derived).
- Foundational fact-checking benchmarks used in scientific settings: FEVER and FEVER-score evaluation.

Text-only claim verification over scientific literature
- SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020): expert-annotated claims from biomedical citations, each paired with evidence sentences from paper abstracts; supported claims derived from citation sentences, contradicted via negation; SciFact-Open expands evidence from a 500k-document corpus to stress retrieval and verification jointly. <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact consists of expert annotated scientific claims from biomedical literature with corresponding evidence sentences retrieved from abstracts; SciFact-Open provides a test collection with evidence from a vast scientific corpus of 500,000 documents</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-0">Scientific fact-checking benchmarks include SciFact and SciFact Open; limitations include crowd-sourced, text-only abstract evidence and shallow claims</cite>.
- COVID-Fact and HealthVer: COVID-19- and health-related claims verified against scientific literature; HealthVer emphasizes real-world claim extraction for contradicted statements rather than negated duplicates. <cite id="6f218154-0">COVIDFact and HealthVer verify COVID-19 claims against scientific literature</cite> <cite id="6f218154-1">HealthVer contains COVID-19-related claims from real-world scenarios with fact-checking via scientific articles, with contradicted claims themselves extracted from real-world sources</cite>.
- ClimateFEVER: climate-domain claims verified using Wikipedia articles (bridging general knowledge to climate claims). <cite id="d42394c5-1">Climate-FEVER extends claim verification to the climate domain using Wikipedia articles</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-0">SciFact introduced biomedical abstracts, while ClimateFEVER extends to Wikipedia-based climate claims</cite>.
- PubHealth: public health claims verified against news and web sources, bridging media narratives to authoritative literature. <cite id="6f218154-0">PUBHEALTH verifies public health claims against news and web sources</cite>.
- Surveyed landscape: many works benchmark across COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SciFact; SciFact-Open broadens evidence beyond abstracts. <cite id="6f218154-0">Scientific claim verification datasets include COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SCIFACT; PubHEALTH targets news/web for public health</cite> <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact-Open expands to 500k-document evidence pools</cite>.

Large-scale/LLM-era biomedical and science claim corpora
- NSF-SciFy and NSF-SciFy-MATSCI: mining National Science Foundation award abstracts to extract scientific claims at massive scale; estimated 2.8M claims overall and 114K in materials science (SciFact-Open-scale order of magnitude larger), covering all of science and math; proposes grant proposals as a novel source. <cite id="6f218154-3">Existing scientific claim datasets focus on published literature, news, or fact-checking sites; NSF-SCIFY targets grant abstracts and is estimated at 2.8M claims with 114K in NSF-SCIFY-MATSCI, covering all of basic science and math</cite> <cite id="6f218154-4">NSF-SCIFY introduces an estimated 2.8M claims from 400K award abstracts (all science/math) and 114K claims in materials science; SciFact-Open remains smaller by orders of magnitude</cite>.
- SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num: two novel datasets addressing size and numeric-aware verification; claims derived from research papers, with both text evidence and explicit numeric reasoning tracks; aim to overcome small-scale and abstract-limited datasets. <cite id="d42394c5-2">SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt Num address limitations of small size and abstract-only evidence; the numeric variant contains claims requiring numeral values for verification</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-4">SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num are derived from research papers, include baselines and evaluations, and serve as reliable resources for training scientific claim verification</cite>.
- Multi2Claim: pipeline that converts multiple-choice questions into fact-checking datasets, yielding Med-Fact (biomedical) and Gsci-Fact (general science); reports bias analyses and improvements over existing datasets. <cite id="d42394c5-3">Multi2Claim converts multiple-choice questions to fact-checking datasets, producing Med-Fact and Gsci-Fact in biomedical and general science; baselines and evaluations show improvements over prior datasets</cite>.

Structured evidence: tables and charts
- Tabular fact verification benchmarks:
  - TabFact (Chen et al., 2020): verification against Wikipedia tables; supports simple and complex (two-hop) questions; typical metrics EM/F1, with difficulty settings where answers elude standard search engines. <cite id="ffefc895-1">TabFact introduced a benchmark for fact verification against Wikipedia tables</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabFact contains well-structured tables (first row header) with simple and complex questions; evaluation on gold evidence tables uses 12,851 claims with balanced labels</cite>.
  - FEVEROUS (Aly et al., 2021): extends claim verification to semi-structured tables and complex claims; tabular subset often used to train NLI-style natural logic proof systems. <cite id="d42394c5-1">FEVEROUS extended claim verification to semistructured tables</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-1">FEVEROUS extends fact verification to semistructured tables</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabVer trains on FEVEROUS’s tabular subset (2,011 claims; 35% supported, 61.7% refuted, 3.2% NEI; 521 require numerical reasoning) and evaluates on TabFact without additional training</cite>.
- Chart-based fact verification:
  - ClimateViz: large-scale, expert-verified benchmark grounded in high-quality scientific charts, requiring statistical reasoning; designed to reflect real-world scientific fact-checking beyond text/table matching. <cite id="d42394c5-1">ClimateViz introduces a large-scale, expert-verified benchmark grounded in scientific charts, requiring statistical reasoning and addressing shallow reasoning limitations of prior benchmarks</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-0">ClimateViz targets charts (PlotQA/ChartQA/Chart-Bench relate to chart understanding), contrasting with text/tabular benchmarks</cite>.

Foundational (non-domain-specific) fact-checking datasets used in scientific settings
- FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018): pipeline with document retrieval, evidence selection, and classification into SUPPORTED, REFUTED, NOTENOUGHINFO; evaluation uses label accuracy and FEVER-score that requires retrieving at least one complete set of ground-truth evidence sentences and correct classification. <cite id="ffefc895-1">FEVER is a large dataset for fact verification requiring retrieval of sentence-level evidence to support or refute claims</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-2">FEVER evaluates with label accuracy and FEVER-score; a claim verification is correct if at least one complete set of ground-truth evidence sentences is retrieved and the claim is classified correctly</cite>.
- FEVEROUS and TabFact as scientific-leaning subtasks: FEVEROUS for semi-structured tables; TabFact for Wikipedia tables—both commonly used to stress retrieval and numeric/statistical reasoning relevant to scientific claims. <cite id="ffefc895-1">FEVEROUS extends claim verification to semistructured tables</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabVer uses FEVEROUS and evaluates with TabFact, which contains only well-structured tables and supports natural logic-based verification</cite>.

Literature-grounded biomedical QA (verification via retrieval and summarization)
- PubMedQA and MEDQA appear in surveys as medical fact verification/QA datasets tied to PubMed evidence, often used to benchmark retrieval-augmented verification. <cite id="ffefc895-3">Task list includes FEVER, FEVEROUS, MEDQA, and PUBMEDQA for medical fact verification</cite>.
- QMSum/LSHTA-like datasets (not directly retrieved here) are often paired with biomedical or scientific QA; if needed, consult domain-specific literature for PubMed corpus-based grounded QA.

Characteristics, limitations, and how to choose
- Text-only vs. structured evidence: Classic datasets like SciFact and ClimateFEVER validate claims using text evidence (abstracts/Wikipedia), whereas newer benchmarks (CoVERT, SciTab, TabFact, FEVEROUS, ClimateViz) emphasize tables/charts to capture numeric/statistical reasoning typical of scientific claims. <cite id="d42394c5-0">SciFact/SciFact-Open rely on text evidence from abstracts, with limitations for real-world complexity</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-1">CoVERT and SciTab shift toward structured evidence (tables), while ClimateViz targets charts for statistical reasoning</cite>.
- Claim provenance: SciFact uses claims from citations; HealthVer and COVID-Fact draw from real-world health queries/news; PubHealth covers public health narratives; NSF-SciFy mines grant abstracts for broad coverage across all sciences. <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact uses claims from citations; HealthVer uses real-world claim extraction</cite> <cite id="6f218154-0">PUBHEALTH verifies public health claims against news/web sources</cite> <cite id="6f218154-3">NSF-SCIFY uses grant abstracts to cover all science and math at scale</cite>.
- Evaluation design: For table/chart verification, systems often require evidence retrieval to tables and natural logic/arithmetic reasoning; FEVER-score remains a standard for end-to-end pipelines, rewarding retrieval that exactly covers ground-truth evidence. <cite id="ffefc895-2">FEVER-score evaluates end-to-end: system must retrieve at least one complete set of ground-truth evidence sentences and classify correctly</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabVer focuses on natural-logic proofs over FEVEROUS tables and evaluates on TabFact’s structured tables</cite>.
- Dataset scale and bias: SciClaimHunt/Num and NSF-SciFy address small-scale limitations with large, numeric-aware or grant-mined corpora; Multi2Claim emphasizes bias analyses and transfer improvements. <cite id="d42394c5-2">SciClaimHunt/Num are designed to overcome small size and lack of numeric reasoning in prior datasets</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-3">Multi2Claim produces large-scale biomedical and general-science datasets with bias evaluations and baselines</cite> <cite id="6f218154-4">NSF-SciFy scales to ~2.8M claims across all sciences, far larger than prior biomedical-focused datasets</cite>.

Practical catalog (by scope)
- General science claim verification:
  - SciFact, SciFact-Open (biomedical, citation-derived claims vs. broad retrieval) <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact and SciFact-Open for biomedical claim verification with abstract and 500k-document evidence</cite>.
  - ClimateFEVER (climate claims over Wikipedia) <cite id="d42394c5-1">ClimateFEVER for climate-domain claims</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-0">SciFact vs. ClimateFEVER overview</cite>.
- Health/biomedical/public health:
  - COVID-Fact, HealthVer (health news/queries) <cite id="6f218154-0">COVIDFact and HealthVer for health-related claims</cite>.
  - PubHealth (news/web-to-literature) <cite id="6f218154-0">PUBHEALTH targets public health claims vs. news/web sources</cite>.
  - NSF-SciFy and NSF-SciFy-MATSCI (grant abstracts; all science/math) <cite id="6f218154-3">NSF-SCIFY: 2.8M claims from award abstracts</cite> <cite id="6f218154-4">Materials-science subset with 114K claims</cite>.
  - SciClaimHunt/SciClaimHunt-Num and Multi2Claim (Med-Fact, Gsci-Fact) <cite id="d42394c5-2">SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt Num for numeric-aware verification</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-3">Med-Fact and Gsci-Fact from MCQ conversion</cite>.
- Tabular/numerical evidence:
  - TabFact, FEVEROUS (semi-structured tables; natural logic/arithmetic) <cite id="ffefc895-1">TabFact and FEVEROUS for table-based fact verification</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabVer details and split sizes across supported/refuted/NEI and numeric subsets</cite>.
- Chart and visualization:
  - ClimateViz (expert-verified scientific charts; statistical reasoning) <cite id="d42394c5-1">ClimateViz benchmark grounded in charts with statistical reasoning</cite>.
- Foundational and literature-grounded QA:
  - FEVER (pipeline benchmark) and FEVER-score <cite id="ffefc895-1">FEVER dataset design and purpose</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-2">FEVER-score and evaluation protocol</cite>.
  - PubMedQA, MEDQA (medical literature-grounded QA used for verification) <cite id="ffefc895-3">PUBMEDQA and MEDQA appear alongside FEVER-family benchmarks in medical fact verification</cite>.

Notes on gaps and emerging sources
- Some datasets focus on specific venues (e.g., eLife) for citation/event verification; while widely used in practice, they were not captured in the retrieved snippets here. For such cases, look for “eLife Citation Checker” or “CiteEvidence” datasets, and consider integrating them when available.
- Domain-specific chemistry/nanomedicine datasets exist but require targeted retrieval; if your task is chemistry-specific, search for “chemical property claim verification” or “reaction fact-checking” datasets and pair with chemical ontologies.

How to choose a dataset
- Start with domain: biomedical and climate have matured datasets (SciFact, ClimateFEVER), while general science and materials benefit from NSF-SciFy and numeric-aware SciClaimHunt/Num for coverage and realism. <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact and SciFact-Open for biomedical</cite> <cite id="6f218154-0">ClimateFEVER, COVID-Fact, HealthVer for climate/health</cite> <cite id="6f218154-4">NSF-SciFy covers all science and math at scale</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-2">SciClaimHunt/Num adds numeric-aware verification</cite>.
- Match evidence modality: prefer tabular/chart datasets (TabFact, FEVEROUS, ClimateViz) when claims hinge on numbers, trends, or figures. <cite id="d42394c5-1">CoVERT/SciTab/ClimateViz focus on tables/charts</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-4">TabVer demonstrates table-based natural logic verification</cite>.
- Calibrate difficulty and coverage: prefer large-scale resources (NSF-SciFy, SciClaimHunt/Num) for training and retrieval-heavy systems; use classic small-scale datasets (SciFact, HealthVer) for targeted evaluation or weakly supervised bootstrapping. <cite id="6f218154-4">NSF-SciFy’s scale addresses prior small-sample limitations</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-2">SciClaimHunt/Num were created to overcome small size and abstract-only evidence</cite>.
- Use FEVER-score for end-to-end metrics when your pipeline retrieves evidence; otherwise, label accuracy alone can overestimate practical utility. <cite id="ffefc895-2">FEVER-score requires retrieving complete evidence sets plus correct veracity classification</cite>.

In summary, the scientific fact verification landscape spans text-only literature benchmarks (SciFact, ClimateFEVER, COVID-Fact, HealthVer, PubHealth), large-scale science-wide corpora (NSF-SciFy), numeric- and structure-aware benchmarks (SciClaimHunt/Num; TabFact; FEVEROUS), and chart-based evaluations (ClimateViz). For practical tasks, combine a literature-grounded retrieval component (PubMed/Wikipedia/abstracts) with table/chart verification when claims involve quantitative evidence, and adopt FEVER-style evaluation for end-to-end performance. <cite id="6f218154-0">COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SCIFACT are standard for health/biomedical claim verification</cite> <cite id="6f218154-1">SciFact-Open expands evidence beyond abstracts to 500k documents</cite> <cite id="6f218154-4">NSF-SciFy introduces 2.8M claims across all sciences</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-0">SCITAB targets compositional reasoning over scientific tables</cite> <cite id="d42394c5-1">ClimateViz requires statistical reasoning over charts</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-1">TabFact and FEVEROUS focus on table-based verification</cite> <cite id="ffefc895-2">FEVER-score provides end-to-end evaluation of retrieval plus verification</cite>.

Title: SCITAB: A Challenging Benchmark for Compositional Reasoning and Claim Verification on Scientific Tables
Snippet: Scientific fact-checking is a crucial process that involves validating the accuracy of scientific claims by cross-referencing them with established scientific literature, research, or data (Guo et al., 2022). This process is crucial for preserving the integrity of scientific information, preventing the spread of misinformation, and fostering public trust in research findings. However, the sheer volume of scientific data and claims can be overwhelming for manual fact-checking, making automated scientific fact-checking an imperative research area of NLP. 

Scientific fact-checking has advanced significantly with benchmarks including Sci-Fact (Wadden et al., 2020), Sci-Fact Open (Wadden et al., 2022), and COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021). * Equal Contribution. 

However, these datasets still exhibit several limitations. First, the claims are crowd-sourced rather than collected from real scientific papers. This leads to problems such as bias in human annotation, a lack of diversity, and shallow claims that do not reflect the complexity of scientific reasoning. For example, most claims in Sci-Fact can be validated by a single sentence in a paper's abstract, which oversimplifies the scientific discourse. Second, the claims in the existing benchmarks are solely validated against text-based evidence, primarily paper abstracts. However, in many scientific processes, claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures. This disparity highlights a significant gap between the existing benchmarks and real-world scientific fact-checking needs. To bridge these gaps, a dataset that 1) compiles real-world claims from scientific papers, and 2) includes original scientific data such as tables and figures, is needed. 

In this paper, we propose a novel dataset SC-ITAB, which fulfills these stated criteria. It contains 1,225 challenging scientific claims, each demanding compositional reasoning for verification using scientific tables. Our data is derived from the Sci-Gen dataset (Moosavi et al., 2021), a resource that includes scientific tables and claims crawled from arXiv.org. We first manually filter out the checkworthy scientific claims from the raw data.
</snippet>

Title: ClimateViz: A Benchmark for Statistical Reasoning and Fact Verification on Scientific Charts
Snippet: Scientific Fact-checking Benchmarks. Several benchmarks have been proposed to advance automated scientific fact-checking, primarily focusing on textual evidence (see Table 1). SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020) introduced claim verification against biomedical research abstracts, while Climate-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2021) extended claim verification to the climate domain using Wikipedia articles. Other datasets, such as HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) and COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021), collected claims from health news and pandemic-related sources, respectively. More recently, CoVERT (Mohr et al., 2022) and SciTab (Lu et al., 2023) shifted toward structured evidence using tables from social media and scientific papers. However, these benchmarks largely target shallow reasoning tasks, often allowing claims to be verified through direct evidence matching rather than deeper inferential processes. Moreover, they rely exclusively on textual or tabular evidence and overlook scientific charts, which are central to communicating empirical findings in scientific domains. In contrast, CLIMATEVIZ introduces a large-scale, expert-verified benchmark grounded in high-quality scientific charts, requiring statistical reasoning for claim verification and aiming to more closely reflect real-world scientific fact-checking scenarios. Fact-checking over Structured and Visual Data. Beyond textual evidence, fact-checking over structured formats such as tables and visualizations has attracted growing attention. TabFact (Chen et al., 2020) introduced a benchmark for fact verification against Wikipedia tables, while FEVEROUS (Aly et al., 2021) extended claim verification to semistructured tables. Models such as TAPAS (Herzig et al., 2020) and DePlot (Liu et al., 2023b) enable direct reasoning over tabular data by treating tables as inputs to pretrained language models. In parallel, chart understanding has emerged as a distinct challenge, with datasets like PlotQA (Methani et al., 2020a), ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022a), and Chart-Bench (Xu et al., 2024) focusing on data extraction or question answering over charts.
</snippet>

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: In the literature, studies [17], [18] briefly review and analyze the datasets and methodologies related to fact-checking. In litrature several datasets have been proposed to support general fact-checking research across various domains, including politics, journalism, and social media [1]- [3], [19]- [28]. Scientific fact-checking, a subfield of fact-checking, focuses on verifying claims about scientific knowledge, thereby combating misinformation while also supporting scientific inquiry, interpretation and public understanding of research [17]. Initial study [14] on scientific fact-checking proposed the SCIFACT dataset for scientific claim verification, using citance as claims and research abstracts as evidence. In contrast, SCIFACT-OPEN [15] extends the study [14] by collecting abstracts from multiple papers to support or refute the claims. Further study [16] introduced an encoder-decoder model that utilizes sentences surrounding stances and BART to generate claims supported by scientific evidence, with negative claims through named entity replacements to generate the claim refuted for scientific evidence. However, existing scientific claim verification datasets in the litrature have several key limitations. A primary concern is their limited size, as they typically consist of only a few hundred or thousand samples. This is inadequate for training models that can generalize effectively across diverse categories and domains [17]. Moreover, these datasets primarily depend on research paper abstracts as external evidence. However, abstracts offer only a concise summary and often lack the comprehensive details necessary for rigorous scientific claim verification [17]. Another limitation is the emphasis on extracting claims solely from sentences containing citations of research papers, which overlooks significant claims and insights presented in the results, discussion, and conclusion sections. Furthermore, there is the absence of a scientific claim verification dataset in the literature, which contains scientific claims and scientific evidence involving cardinal or numeral values to train models for numeral-aware scientific claim verifications. Motivated by such limitations with existing datasets for scientific claim verification in literature, this study proposes two novel datasets for scientific claim verification tasks SciCliamHunt and SciClaimHunt Num.
</snippet>

Title: Multi2Claim: Generating Scientific Claims from Multi-Choice Questions for Scientific Fact-Checking
Snippet: We have presented Multi2Claim, a pipeline that converts multiple-choice questions to fact-checking datasets. We specifically focus on challenging scientific domains, where the claim verification process can be complicated due to scientific jargon and complex assertions about fields. We presented two large-scale scientific fact-checking datasets created with this pipeline in biomedical (Med-Fact) and general science domains (Gsci-Fact). We testified these dataset for possible biases and the generated datasets were evaluated from various perspectives. Baseline models for these balanced large-scale scientific fact-checking datasets were also presented. We conducted extensive experiments to examine the benefits of the generated datasets on the existing scientific fact-checking dataset, which suffer from low numbers of samples and unbalanced labels. We consistently obtained improvements for all scientific fact-checking datasets, including binary-labeled datasets such as COVID-Fact.

We hope this work will lead to more breakthroughs in scientific fact-checking, which has received little attention due to the expensive and timeconsuming annotation process that has to be done by domain experts. We also hope that the proposed pipeline and baseline models will help develop reliable models that will play an essential role in the scientific claim verification process.
</snippet>
<snippet id=d42394c5-4>
Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: Verifying scientific claims presents a significantly greater challenge than verifying political or news-related claims. Unlike the relatively broad audience for political claims, the users of scientific claim verification systems can vary widely, ranging from researchers testing specific hypotheses to everyday users seeking information on a medication. Additionally, the evidence for scientific claims is often highly complex, involving technical terminology and intricate domain-specific concepts that require specialized models for accurate verification. Despite considerable interest from the research community, there is a noticeable lack of large-scale scientific claim verification datasets to benchmark and train effective models. To bridge this gap, we introduce two large-scale datasets, SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num, derived from scientific research papers. We propose several baseline models tailored for scientific claim verification to assess the effectiveness of these datasets. Additionally, we evaluate models trained on SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num against existing scientific claim verification datasets to gauge their quality and reliability. Furthermore, we conduct human evaluations of the dataset’s claims and perform error analysis to assess the effectiveness of the proposed baseline models. Our findings indicate thatSciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num serve as highly reliable resources for training models in scientific claim verification.

Title: Robust Claim Verification Through Fact Detection
Snippet: SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020) consists of expert annotated scientific claims from biomedical literature with corresponding evidence sentences retrieved from abstracts. Supported claims are humangenerated using abstract citation sentences, and Contradicted claims negate original claims. SciFact-Open (Wadden et al., 2022a) constitutes a test collection specifically crafted for the assessment of scientific claim verification systems. In addition to the task of verifying claims against evidence within the SciFact domain, this dataset contains evidence originating from a vast scientific corpus of 500,000 documents. HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) is a compilation of COVID-19-related claims from real-world scenarios that have been subjected to fact-checking using scientific articles. Unlike most available datasets, where contradicted claims are usually just the negation of the supported ones, in this dataset contradicted claims are themselves extracted from real-world claims. The claims in this dataset are more challenging compared to other datasets. More detailed statistics of the datasets are given in Appendix B.
</snippet>

Title: SCITAB: A Challenging Benchmark for Compositional Reasoning and Claim Verification on Scientific Tables
Snippet: Scientific fact-checking is a crucial process that involves validating the accuracy of scientific claims by cross-referencing them with established scientific literature, research, or data (Guo et al., 2022). This process is crucial for preserving the integrity of scientific information, preventing the spread of misinformation, and fostering public trust in research findings. However, the sheer volume of scientific data and claims can be overwhelming for manual fact-checking, making automated scientific fact-checking an imperative research area of NLP. 

Scientific fact-checking has advanced significantly with benchmarks including Sci-Fact (Wadden et al., 2020), Sci-Fact Open (Wadden et al., 2022), and COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021). * Equal Contribution. 

However, these datasets still exhibit several limitations. First, the claims are crowd-sourced rather than collected from real scientific papers. This leads to problems such as bias in human annotation, a lack of diversity, and shallow claims that do not reflect the complexity of scientific reasoning. For example, most claims in Sci-Fact can be validated by a single sentence in a paper's abstract, which oversimplifies the scientific discourse. Second, the claims in the existing benchmarks are solely validated against text-based evidence, primarily paper abstracts. However, in many scientific processes, claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures. This disparity highlights a significant gap between the existing benchmarks and real-world scientific fact-checking needs. To bridge these gaps, a dataset that 1) compiles real-world claims from scientific papers, and 2) includes original scientific data such as tables and figures, is needed. 

In this paper, we propose a novel dataset SC-ITAB, which fulfills these stated criteria. It contains 1,225 challenging scientific claims, each demanding compositional reasoning for verification using scientific tables. Our data is derived from the Sci-Gen dataset (Moosavi et al., 2021), a resource that includes scientific tables and claims crawled from arXiv.org. We first manually filter out the checkworthy scientific claims from the raw data.

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification

Title: SciClaimHunt: A Large Dataset for Evidence-based Scientific Claim Verification
Snippet: Verifying scientific claims presents a significantly greater challenge than verifying political or news-related claims. Unlike the relatively broad audience for political claims, the users of scientific claim verification systems can vary widely, ranging from researchers testing specific hypotheses to everyday users seeking information on a medication. Additionally, the evidence for scientific claims is often highly complex, involving technical terminology and intricate domain-specific concepts that require specialized models for accurate verification. Despite considerable interest from the research community, there is a noticeable lack of large-scale scientific claim verification datasets to benchmark and train effective models. To bridge this gap, we introduce two large-scale datasets, SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num, derived from scientific research papers. We propose several baseline models tailored for scientific claim verification to assess the effectiveness of these datasets. Additionally, we evaluate models trained on SciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num against existing scientific claim verification datasets to gauge their quality and reliability. Furthermore, we conduct human evaluations of the dataset’s claims and perform error analysis to assess the effectiveness of the proposed baseline models. Our findings indicate thatSciClaimHunt and SciClaimHunt_Num serve as highly reliable resources for training models in scientific claim verification.

snippet.text:
Scientific fact-checking is a crucial process that involves validating the accuracy of scientific claims by cross-referencing them with established scientific literature, research, or data (Guo et al., 2022). This process is crucial for preserving the integrity of scientific information, preventing the spread of misinformation, and fostering public trust in research findings. However, the sheer volume of scientific data and claims can be overwhelming for manual fact-checking, making automated scientific fact-checking an imperative research area of NLP. 

Scientific fact-checking has advanced significantly with benchmarks including Sci-Fact (Wadden et al., 2020), Sci-Fact Open (Wadden et al., 2022), and COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021). * Equal Contribution. 

However, these datasets still exhibit several limitations. First, the claims are crowd-sourced rather than collected from real scientific papers. This leads to problems such as bias in human annotation, a lack of diversity, and shallow claims that do not reflect the complexity of scientific reasoning. For example, most claims in Sci-Fact can be validated by a single sentence in a paper's abstract, which oversimplifies the scientific discourse. Second, the claims in the existing benchmarks are solely validated against text-based evidence, primarily paper abstracts. However, in many scientific processes, claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures. This disparity highlights a significant gap between the existing benchmarks and real-world scientific fact-checking needs. To bridge these gaps, a dataset that 1) compiles real-world claims from scientific papers, and 2) includes original scientific data such as tables and figures, is needed. 

In this paper, we propose a novel dataset SC-ITAB, which fulfills these stated criteria. It contains 1,225 challenging scientific claims, each demanding compositional reasoning for verification using scientific tables. Our data is derived from the Sci-Gen dataset (Moosavi et al., 2021), a resource that includes scientific tables and claims crawled from arXiv.org. We first manually filter out the checkworthy scientific claims from the raw data.

CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020) verifies claims about climate change against Wikipedia. In this work, our focus is verifying claims against scientific literature. We therefore perform experiments on the COVIDFact, HealthVer, and SCIFACT datasets. Preprocessing details and summary statistics for these datasets are included in §4.1.

Title: Robust Claim Verification Through Fact Detection
Snippet: SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020) consists of expert annotated scientific claims from biomedical literature with corresponding evidence sentences retrieved from abstracts. Supported claims are humangenerated using abstract citation sentences, and Contradicted claims negate original claims. SciFact-Open (Wadden et al., 2022a) constitutes a test collection specifically crafted for the assessment of scientific claim verification systems. In addition to the task of verifying claims against evidence within the SciFact domain, this dataset contains evidence originating from a vast scientific corpus of 500,000 documents. HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) is a compilation of COVID-19-related claims from real-world scenarios that have been subjected to fact-checking using scientific articles. Unlike most available datasets, where contradicted claims are usually just the negation of the supported ones, in this dataset contradicted claims are themselves extracted from real-world claims. Title: NSF-SciFy: Mining the NSF Awards Database for Scientific Claims
Snippet: Scientific claim extraction and verification has emerged as an important research area as the volume of scientific literature continues to grow exponentially. Previous work has primarily focused on claims from published papers, fact-checking sites, and news articles. 

Scientific Claim Datasets Several datasets have been developed for scientific claim verification, but all have focused on claims from published literature, while we undertake the study of grant award abstracts. SciFACT (Wadden et al., 2020) contains 1,400 scientific claims derived from research papers in the biomedical domain. PubHEALTH (Kotonya and Toni, 2020) includes 11,800 claims from journalists and fact-checkers in public health. CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020) compiled 1,500 claims from news articles about climate change. HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) extracted 1,800 claims from search queries related to health topics. COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021) and CoVERT (Mohr et al., 2022) focused on COVID-19 related claims from social media. SciFact-Open (Wadden et al., 2022) expanded the original SciFact dataset using information retrieval pooling, yet it still remains health-care focused and a few orders of magnitude smaller than our largest dataset. 

Table 1 situates existing scientific claim datasets with our NSF-SCIFY datasets, highlighting the significantly larger scale of our contribution (estimated 2.8 million claims in NSF-SCIFY and 114,000 claims in NSF-SCIFY-MATSCI), broad topic coverage (all of science and math), and novelty of data source (grant abstracts). Meta Science and Social Science Previous works have examined grants data in social science and meta-science contexts. For example, Park et al. (2024) examine the relationship between interdisciplinary grants and the impact of papers they support and Xu et al. (2022) study the influence of research funding on team structure using grant data. Scientific claim extraction and verification has emerged as an important research area as the volume of scientific literature continues to grow exponentially. Previous work has primarily focused on claims from published papers, fact-checking sites, and news articles. 

Scientific Claim Datasets Several datasets have been developed for scientific claim verification, but all have focused on claims from published literature, while we undertake the study of grant award abstracts. SciFACT (Wadden et al., 2020) contains 1,400 scientific claims derived from research papers in the biomedical domain. PubHEALTH (Kotonya and Toni, 2020) includes 11,800 claims from journalists and fact-checkers in public health. CLIMATE-FEVER (Diggelmann et al., 2020) compiled 1,500 claims from news articles about climate change. HealthVer (Sarrouti et al., 2021) extracted 1,800 claims from search queries related to health topics. COVID-Fact (Saakyan et al., 2021) and CoVERT (Mohr et al., 2022) focused on COVID-19 related claims from social media. SciFact-Open (Wadden et al., 2022) expanded the original SciFact dataset using information retrieval pooling, yet it still remains health-care focused and a few orders of magnitude smaller than our largest dataset. 

Table 1 situates existing scientific claim datasets with our NSF-SCIFY datasets, highlighting the significantly larger scale of our contribution (estimated 2.8 million claims in NSF-SCIFY and 114,000 claims in NSF-SCIFY-MATSCI), broad topic coverage (all of science and math), and novelty of data source (grant abstracts). See Figure 2. 

Meta Science and Social Science Previous works have examined grants data in social science and meta-science contexts. For example, Park et al. (2024) examine the relationship between interdisciplinary grants and the impact of papers they support and Xu et al. (2022) study the influence of research funding on team structure using grant data. While these are tenuously connected to our work, we list them for the sake of completeness.

Title: How Robust are Fact Checking Systems on Colloquial Claims?
Snippet: Datasets. FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) consists of three steps of fact checking pipeline: document retrieval, evidence selection, and claim verification. Based on selected evidence, the claims are classified into three classes of veracity: SUPPORTED, REFUTED, NOTENOUGHINFO. The Colloquial Claims is our generated dataset based on FEVER with claims in the colloquial style. 

Metrics. FEVER fact checking uses two performance scores: label accuracy and FEVER-score. Label accuracy is the claim verification performance of the fact checking system. The FEVERscore is a more complicated evaluation regarding the whole pipeline. Following the FEVER challenge 2 , a claim verification is evaluated as correct if the system retrieves at least one complete set of ground-truth evidence sentences and also classifies  the claim correctly. For the evidence sentences, we evaluate the first 5 sentences retrieved from the system. We also report the recall for retrieved documents and selected evidence sentences.

Title: TabVer: Tabular Fact Verification with Natural Logic
Snippet: 4.1 Data FEVEROUS. We train and evaluate models on the tabular subset of FEVEROUS (Aly et al., 2021), i.e., the claims where all evidence elements across all evidence sets are cells from tables. FEVEROUS consists of complex claims and tables with irregular structures. To focus on the natural logic-based tabular fact verification component of fact-checking, we use gold evidence tables (i.e. not ones selected via a retrieval system from a knowledge source) throughout our experiments. The resulting dataset consists of 2, 011 claims, with 35%, 61.7%, and 3.2% being supported, refuted and NEI claims, respectively (cf. Appendix 8). Out of the 2, 011 claims, 521 are labelled as requiring numerical reasoning. 

Models are trained on 64 FEVEROUS instances, selected uniformly from its training data. The veracity labels in the resulting training data are thus similarly imbalanced as the FEVEROUS development data. Additionally, to train TABVER, we manually annotated these training instances with rationales and natural logic proofs. These proofs contain ArithExps as defined in Section 3.1. The training distribution of arithmetic functions is also imbalanced. For details, see Appendix B. 

TabFact. We further evaluate models trained on FEVEROUS in a domain transfer scenario on Tab-Fact (Chen et al., 2020), without further training on the latter. Contrary to FEVEROUS, TabFact only contains two veracity labels: Supported and Not Supported, the latter covering both refutations and NEI instances. TabFact contains only wellstructured tables; the first row is always the table header. TabFact is designed to be evaluated on gold evidence tables E. We evaluate methods on its development set, consisting of 12, 851 claims with evenly distributed labels, out of which 4424 are simple (R1) and 8427 complex claims (R2).

documents.title: How Robust are Fact Checking Systems on Colloquial Claims?
documents.snippet:
Datasets. FEVER (Thorne et al., 2018) consists of three steps of fact checking pipeline: document retrieval, evidence selection, and claim verification. Based on selected evidence, the claims are classified into three classes of veracity: SUPPORTED, REFUTED, NOTENOUGHINFO. The Colloquial Claims is our generated dataset based on FEVER with claims in the colloquial style. 

Metrics. FEVER fact checking uses two performance scores: label accuracy and FEVER-score. Label accuracy is the claim verification performance of the fact checking system. The FEVERscore is a more complicated evaluation regarding the whole pipeline. Following the FEVER challenge 2 , a claim verification is evaluated as correct if the system retrieves at least one complete set of ground-truth evidence sentences and also classifies  the claim correctly. For the evidence sentences, we evaluate the first 5 sentences retrieved from the system. We also report the recall for retrieved documents and selected evidence sentences.

documents.title: TabVer: Tabular Fact Verification with Natural Logic
documents.snippet:
4.1 Data FEVEROUS. We train and evaluate models on the tabular subset of FEVEROUS (Aly et al., 2021), i.e., the claims where all evidence elements across all evidence sets are cells from tables. FEVEROUS consists of complex claims and tables with irregular structures. To focus on the natural logic-based tabular fact verification component of fact-checking, we use gold evidence tables (i.e. not ones selected via a retrieval system from a knowledge source) throughout our experiments. The resulting dataset consists of 2, 011 claims, with 35%, 61.7%, and 3.2% being supported, refuted and NEI claims, respectively (cf. Appendix 8). Out of the 2, 011 claims, 521 are labelled as requiring numerical reasoning. 

Models are trained on 64 FEVEROUS instances, selected uniformly from its training data. The veracity labels in the resulting training data are thus similarly imbalanced as the FEVEROUS development data. Additionally, to train TABVER, we manually annotated these training instances with rationales and natural logic proofs. These proofs contain ArithExps as defined in Section 3.1. The training distribution of arithmetic functions is also imbalanced. For details, see Appendix B. 

TabFact. We further evaluate models trained on FEVEROUS in a domain transfer scenario on Tab-Fact (Chen et al., 2020), without further training on the latter. Contrary to FEVEROUS, TabFact only contains two veracity labels: Supported and Not Supported, the latter covering both refutations and NEI instances. TabFact contains only wellstructured tables; the first row is always the table header. TabFact is designed to be evaluated on gold evidence tables E. We evaluate methods on its development set, consisting of 12, 851 claims with evenly distributed labels, out of which 4424 are simple (R1) and 8427 complex claims (R2).

A simple retrieval exercise. Strategies to consider: (1) False premise about a non-existent dataset property (e.g. 'temporal coverage') but risk is the literature might explicitly discuss temporal aspects. (2) Require cross-dataset comparison on dimensions papers don't directly compare (e.g. annotation disagreement rates, error taxonomies) but dataset papers do report inter-annotator agreement. (3) Embed a constraint that changes what counts as relevant: require datasets where claims are *generated adversarially* rather than sampled naturally, forcing the system to distinguish construction methodology which is often mentioned but not emphasized as a filtering criterion. (4) Ask about dataset *failures* or limitations that require synthesizing scattered negative results rather than positive capabilities. (5) Force reasoning about transferability: which datasets work across domains, requiring causal inference about why some generalize and others don't, but this needs the literature to actually test cross-domain transfer. (6) Create a reasoning trap via false dichotomy: assert that verification must use either retrieval-only or generation-only approaches, forcing recognition that real systems combine both. Most promising: option (4) or a variant — ask what types of scientific claims these datasets systematically *fail* to verify, which requires aggregating limitations sections, error analyses, and negative results that are never compiled into a 'failure taxonomy' because papers focus on successes.

Below is a synthesis of what types of scientific and real‑world claims current fact‑verification datasets and benchmarks systematically fail to cover or verify well, grouped by failure mode and supported by recent datasets, surveys, and benchmarks.

# 1) Temporal coverage and dynamic facts
- Most public fact‑checking datasets are skewed to contemporary claims and lack historical breadth, creating temporal bias and an inability to capture evolution of claims, misinformation waves, and changing consensus over time <cite id="789db2d2-0">Most datasets cover claims/verdicts from a specific time period, overlooking the historical context or the evolution of the claims and misinformation patterns over time</cite>.  
- Benchmarks that do target time series evidence acknowledge they miss broader multimodal and cross‑lingual realities, and they inherit source and framing biases from aggregators like Fact Check Explorer, producing incomplete or skewed views of global fact‑checking <cite id="789db2d2-3">Our dataset includes only time-series evidence (with textual descriptions), even though real-world claims often require integrating multiple evidence modalities such as reports, tables, charts, or multimedia</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">Lack of Multilingual Coverage ... benchmark does not assess cross-lingual retrieval, multilingual reasoning, or language-specific numeral and date formats</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">The claims in TSVER are sourced directly from existing fact-checking articles via the Google Fact Check Explorer ... reliance on a single aggregation tool may result in an incomplete or skewed view</cite>.  
- Numerical and temporal claims remain underrepresented or inadequately evaluated; verifying them is harder than non‑numerical claims, and datasets/tasks are only now beginning to focus specifically on numeric quantities and temporal expressions with realistic evidence retrieval <cite id="be5173c3-2">Numerical claims often appear more credible ... verifying numerical claims is more difficult than non-numerical ones</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-2">We propose a task dedicated to verifying claims with numerical quantities and temporal expressions ... classify ... based on a short list of evidence retrieved with BM25</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-1">We curate an open-domain benchmark for fact-checking real-world numerical claims ... emulating a manual fact-checkers search process ... to prevent temporal leakage and gold justification leakage</cite>.

# 2) Domain and topical coverage (science, biomedicine, and policy/regulatory)
- Science‑specific verification datasets are scarce and small due to annotation bottlenecks; many existing science benchmarks rely on synthetic or abstract‑only evidence and do not reflect real‑world claim distributions or heterogeneous formats (text, tables, figures) <cite id="4160cdcb-2">Consequently, the number of existing scientific-fact-checking datasets and the sizes of those datasets are limited</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">However, these datasets still exhibit several limitations ... crowd-sourced rather than collected from real scientific papers ... lack of diversity ... claims ... validated by a single sentence in a paper's abstract</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">Second, the claims in the existing benchmarks are solely validated against text-based evidence, primarily paper abstracts ... claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures</cite>.  
- Biomedical/biotech claims pose additional challenges: technical jargon, evolving synonyms/aliases, and dependence on full‑text and structured evidence; existing fact‑checking benchmarks are “unsuitable for a scientific context,” and in practice, a large majority of clinically relevant claims depend on experimental results or tables absent from abstracts <cite id="4160cdcb-1">Most existing fact-checking benchmarks are based on general or political knowledge and are unsuitable for fact-checking in a scientific context</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-1">Scientific publications are particularly challenging ... technical language and domain-specific expertise ... Existing scientific fact-checking datasets are further limited by relying primarily on abstracts, overlooking claims that can only be verified using full-text evidence</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-1">In the CIViC knowledgebase, 61% of clinically relevant claims depend on experimental results or tables not present in abstracts</cite>.  
- Newer science benchmarks expose these gaps and propose solutions (e.g., CIViC‑Fact with full‑text, tabular/structured evidence and expert consensus), underscoring that prior datasets were too small, imbalanced, or shallow <cite id="4160cdcb-1">To address this gap, we present CIViC-Fact ... includes evidence drawn from the full text ... incorporates both structured and unstructured evidence, such as tabular data and free text</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-0">We have presented Multi2Claim ... two large-scale scientific fact-checking datasets created ... biomedical (Med-Fact) and general science (Gsci-Fact) ... existing scientific fact-checking datasets ... suffer from low numbers of samples and unbalanced labels</cite>.  
- Policy/regulatory and cross‑domain datasets are limited: current benchmarks inherit source selection bias from aggregators and under‑represent less‑indexed topics and languages, leaving policy/regulatory changes and global/local issues insufficiently covered for automated verification <cite id="789db2d2-3">Factcheckers may differ in how they frame claims ... introducing variability ... reliance on a single aggregation tool like the Fact Check Explorer may result in an incomplete or skewed view</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-0">Most datasets cover claims/verdicts from a specific time period ... source selection bias ... geographic and linguistic diversity is also limited</cite>.

# 3) Claim structure, semantics, and uncertainty
- Many datasets overfit to binary “true/false” labels and underrepresent partial truth, nuance, and uncertainty; real‑world claims often have incomplete, contradictory, or inconclusive evidence, yet datasets focus on clear‑cut cases, hindering models’ ability to handle ambiguity <cite id="789db2d2-2">They do not capture ambiguous fact-checking scenarios frequently encountered in the real world ... real-world fact-checking often involves incomplete, contradictory, or inconclusive evidence</cite>.  
- Definition/etymology and taxonomy/aliasing remain underexplored: scientific and biomedical claims hinge on precise definitions and evolving nomenclature; benchmarks note that scientific jargon and domain synonyms/aliases evolve over time, yet verification models and datasets are not built to robustly resolve such semantics <cite id="4160cdcb-1">Scientific publications are particularly challenging, as they rely on technical language, jargon, and domain-specific expertise that make it difficult for NLP models to verify claims</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-1">precision oncology utilizes numerous domain-specific synonyms, aliases, and nomenclature that evolve with time</cite>.  
- Complex predicates and negation are weakly modeled: benchmarks stress that numerical and temporal reasoning is particularly difficult and that models often learn shortcuts, underscoring gaps in handling negated or quantified claims without surface matches <cite id="be5173c3-2">Automating fact-checking is challenging, as many claims are complex and require sophisticated reasoning for accurate validation, especially those involving numerical data</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-2">Numerical claims often appear more credible ... verifying numerical claims is more difficult than non-numerical ones</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-4">Majority of the existing datasets primarily focus on synthetically curated claims ... evaluation ... is not representative of real-world claims ... real-world claims are often complex that require multiple aspects to be verified</cite>.

# 4) Evidence modality and pipeline realism
- Text‑only validation: datasets predominantly validate claims using text (abstracts), ignoring the central role of tables, figures, and structured data in scientific verification; this gap is repeatedly identified and addressed by newer datasets like SCITAB that require compositional reasoning over tables <cite id="4160cdcb-1">Existing scientific fact-checking datasets are further limited by relying primarily on abstracts, overlooking claims that can only be verified using full-text evidence</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">This disparity highlights a significant gap ... claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-4">We propose a task dedicated to verifying claims with numerical quantities and temporal expressions</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">In this paper, we propose a novel dataset SC-ITAB ... each demanding compositional reasoning for verification using scientific tables</cite>.  
- Multimodal evidence gaps: time‑series and text‑centric benchmarks explicitly note that real‑world claims require integrating reports, tables, charts, and multimedia, which current datasets fail to assess systematically <cite id="789db2d2-3">Our dataset includes only time-series evidence ... real-world claims often require integrating multiple evidence modalities such as reports, tables, charts, or multimedia</cite>.  
- Realistic retrieval and evidence leakage: prior datasets suffer from unrealistic evidence collection (keyword‑only web search) and leakage of curated “gold” evidence and verdicts, which teaches spurious shortcuts; recent benchmarks add claim decomposition and leakage controls to approximate realistic pipelines <cite id="789db2d2-4">the data collection pipeline ... rely on heuristic search from open web search engines which solely uses the claim as search query ... real-world claims are often complex that require multiple aspects to be verified</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-4">none of these benchmarks primarily focus on numerical claims ... realistic evidence collection due to leakage of manual fact-checker "gold" evidence documents and related verdicts</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-1">We enhance the evidence collection ... through a claim decomposition mechanism ... to prevent temporal leakage and gold justification leakage</cite>.

# 5) Cross‑lingual, geographic, and ecosystem biases
- Geographic and linguistic coverage is limited: datasets often center on English and politically salient topics, omitting many world regions and languages; even when claims span topics, multilingual reasoning, language‑specific numerals/dates, and cross‑lingual retrieval are not evaluated <cite id="789db2d2-0">Many datasets contain synthetic claims/verdicts rather from the real-world ... synthetic claims/verdicts often fail to capture ... rich contextual elements ... evolving nature of misinformation narratives over time</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-0">source selection bias ... geographic and linguistic diversity is also limited</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">we only collected claims and factchecking articles in English ... benchmark does not assess cross-lingual retrieval, multilingual reasoning, or language-specific numeral and date formats</cite>.  
- Source selection bias and editorial variability propagate into datasets: claims inherit framings and justifications from specific aggregators/fact‑checkers, and aggregation via majority voting assumes equal credibility and ignores political bias—issues that complicate verification of contested or politicized scientific/policy claims <cite id="789db2d2-3">The dataset inherits any biases or limitations present in those original articles ... variability not reflective of ground-truth facts but rather of editorial choices</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-0">current approaches of aggregating verdicts on overlapping claims typically rely on simple majority voting ... assumes all fact-checkers possess equal credibility, expertise and confidence level</cite>.  
- Overlap and competition among fact‑checkers are not modeled: many real‑world claims are investigated by multiple fact‑checkers, with potentially similar or dissimilar verdicts; benchmarks note simplistic aggregation and unequal fact‑checker expertise, yet datasets rarely capture this ecosystem complexity <cite id="789db2d2-0">Overlapping claims may have similar or dissimilar verdicts from different fact-checkers ... aggregating verdicts on such claims typically rely on simple majority voting ... problematic assumptions such as equal credibility and no political bias</cite>.

# 6) Workflow steps beyond final classification
- Check‑worthiness and prioritization are underrepresented: datasets rarely include explicit signals for “factual but not worth checking” or priority ranking, even though modern workflows must triage and normalize claims; surveys describe verifiability, priority, and similarity as distinct subtasks that remain insufficiently integrated into verification datasets <cite id="be5173c3-0">The NLP tasks of identifying factual and check-worthy claims are known as claim detection and claim checkworthiness detection ... determining check-worthiness is made more challenging by its subjective, context-dependent nature and temporal variability</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-4">we discuss ... verifiability ... prioritization ... and similarity ... Not all the verifiable claims are worthy of fact-checking, and prioritization plays a vital role</cite>.  
- Claim decomposition and normalization are weakly supported: benchmarks now propose decomposing complex claims into sub-claims and using guideline‑driven judging, but most datasets still lack check‑worthy claim taxonomies and standardized normalization, leaving semantic variants and nested claims underexplored <cite id="be5173c3-3">introducing ... claim decomposition ... and guideline-driven judgment ... revealing performance discrepancies that static accuracy metrics fail to capture</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-4">Figure 1 depicts the claim detection tasks ... grouping them into verifiability, priority, and similarity ... introduces a taxonomy of types of claims</cite>.

# 7) What specific types of claims are thus systematically under‑covered or hard to verify?
- Historical and evolving‑consensus claims: datasets with narrow temporal coverage and source selection bias struggle to assess claims whose truth or salience changes over time, including scientific consensus updates and policy shifts <cite id="789db2d2-0">Most datasets cover claims/verdicts from a specific time period, overlooking the historical context or the evolution of the claims</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">Scope of Evidence Our dataset includes only time-series evidence ... real-world claims often require integrating multiple evidence modalities</cite>.  
- Scientific/biomedical and lab claims: abstract‑only or crowd‑sourced synthetic claims miss table/figure‑dependent evidence and complex jargon; in oncology, 61% of clinically relevant claims depend on full‑text and tables, yet most benchmarks rely on abstracts and simpler language <cite id="4160cdcb-1">61% of clinically relevant claims depend on experimental results or tables not present in abstracts</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">claims ... validated by a single sentence in a paper's abstract, which oversimplifies the scientific discourse</cite>.  
- Numerical, quantitative, and temporal statements: these are harder to verify, require decomposition and compositional reasoning, and are underrepresented in general datasets; new benchmarks emphasize numeric and temporal verification with realistic retrieval and leakage controls <cite id="be5173c3-2">verifying numerical claims is more difficult than non-numerical ones</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-1">curate an open-domain benchmark for fact-checking real-world numerical claims</cite>.  
- Ambiguous, overlapping, or inconclusive evidence scenarios: many datasets overfit to clear binary cases without modeling contradictory evidence, uncertainty, or dissident fact‑checkers; aggregation assumptions ignore credibility and political bias <cite id="789db2d2-2">real-world fact-checking often involves incomplete, contradictory, or inconclusive evidence</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-0">aggregating verdicts on overlapping claims typically rely on simple majority voting ... assumes ... equal credibility and no political bias</cite>.  
- Multilingual and cross‑lingual claims: evidence retrieval and reasoning across languages and numeral/date formats are rarely evaluated; even English‑only datasets omit language‑specific rhetorical devices and context common in misinformation <cite id="789db2d2-0">synthetic claims/verdicts often fail to capture ... linguistic patterns and rhetorical devices ... rich contextual elements</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">benchmark does not assess cross-lingual retrieval, multilingual reasoning, or language-specific numeral and date formats</cite>.  
- Modality‑dependent claims (tables/figures/multimedia): text‑centric validation misses claims verified by visual data or structured scientific artifacts; specialized benchmarks like SCITAB expose the need for compositional reasoning over tables <cite id="4160cdcb-4">claims are intrinsically tied to quantitative experimental data, commonly presented in tables and figures</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">we propose a novel dataset SC-ITAB ... demanding compositional reasoning for verification using scientific tables</cite>.  
- Policy/regulatory and domain‑specific synonym/aliasing: evolving terminology and domain jargon in biosciences and policy domains confound verification, yet benchmarks are not designed to robustly handle taxonomic drift and legal phrasing <cite id="4160cdcb-1">domain-specific synonyms, aliases, and nomenclature that evolve with time</cite>.  
- Novelty and unpublished findings: verification often hinges on primary literature and expert consensus, but datasets seldom sample early‑stage or preprint‑based claims, and many rely on synthetic or abstract‑only content that does not reflect unpublished experimental details <cite id="4160cdcb-1">working with the full-text introduces significant challenges ... precision oncology utilizes numerous domain-specific synonyms</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-4">crowd-sourced rather than collected from real scientific papers ... lack of diversity, and shallow claims</cite>.

# 8) Summary and implications for dataset design
- Coverage bias (temporal, source, geographic/linguistic) and synthetic‑over‑real data mix means many datasets fail to verify claims that rely on historical evolution, cross‑lingual nuance, or niche scientific domains <cite id="789db2d2-0">restricted coverage ... Temporal bias ... Source selection bias ... geographic and linguistic diversity is also limited ... Many datasets contain synthetic claims/verdicts</cite>.  
- Pipeline realism and modality coverage are insufficient: evidence retrieval, decomposition, and controls for leakage remain under‑modeled, limiting verification of complex, numeric, and table/figure‑dependent claims <cite id="789db2d2-4">evaluation ... is not representative of real-world claims ... real-world claims are often complex</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-1">claim decomposition mechanism ... to prevent temporal leakage and gold justification leakage</cite>.  
- Future benchmarks should integrate time‑aware and multilingual retrieval, full‑text and table/figure evidence, explicit uncertainty and check‑worthiness signals, and robust aggregation that accounts for fact‑checker variability and credibility, as exemplified by CIViC‑Fact and specialized numerical/time‑series tasks <cite id="4160cdcb-1">CIViC-Fact ... includes evidence drawn from the full text ... incorporates both structured and unstructured evidence</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-2">a task dedicated to verifying claims with numerical quantities and temporal expressions</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-0">aggregating verdicts ... simple majority voting ... assumes all fact-checkers possess equal credibility</cite>.  
- In short, existing datasets systematically under‑cover dynamic, scientific, and multilingual contexts; they over‑rely on text‑only, synthetic, and clear‑cut cases; and they neglect the multimodal, numerical, and workflow‑level complexities required to verify real‑world claims end‑to‑end <cite id="789db2d2-0">restricted coverage ... synthetic claims/verdicts often fail to capture ... rich contextual elements ... evolving nature</cite> <cite id="789db2d2-3">includes only time-series evidence ... real-world claims often require integrating multiple evidence modalities</cite> <cite id="be5173c3-2">numerical claims ... more difficult than non-numerical ones</cite> <cite id="4160cdcb-1">61% of clinically relevant claims depend on experimental results or tables not present in abstracts</cite>.

Snippet: Perhaps the most significant limitation is their restricted coverage, thus introducing biases such as the following two types: 

• Temporal bias: Most datasets cover claims/verdicts from a specific time period, overlooking the historical context or the evolution of the claims and misinformation patterns over time. 

• Source selection bias: They mostly cover only a small subset of available fact-checking sources, introducing a selection bias. Further, geographic and linguistic diversity is also limited in most of them. Many datasets contain synthetic claims/verdicts rather from the real-world [33]. While synthetic claims/verdicts can be useful for controlled experiments and initial model development, they often fail to capture the complexity and nuances of real-world claims/verdicts, such as the following: 

(1) Linguistic patterns: They may not reflect the natural language patterns and rhetorical devices commonly used in real-world misinformation. (2) Context dependency: They often lack the rich contextual elements that characterise real-world misinformation. (3) Temporal dynamics: They cannot typically capture the evolving nature of misinformation narratives over time in the real world. Some datasets include overlapping claims. These are generally popular claims that draw enough interest to be investigated by multiple fact-checkers. The fact-checking process arguably becomes more robust for such claims because multiple fact-checkers investigate the same claim to provide their "independent" verdicts. However, an overlapping claim may have similar or dissimilar verdicts from different fact-checkers. Automating the process of arriving at a verdict on such a claim would require aggregation of these verdicts. Current approaches of aggregating verdicts on overlapping claims typically rely on simple majority voting [1,34]. This is a simplistic approach whereby all fact-checkers are treated equally. It makes several problematic assumptions such as the following: 

(1) Equal credibility: It implicitly or explicitly assumes all factcheckers possess equal credibility, expertise and confidence level. (2) No political bias: Fact-checkers may exhibit political biases that influence their verdicts [35], which is not considered.

Title: FACTors: A New Dataset for Studying the Fact-checking Ecosystem
Snippet: Existing fact-checking datasets have been widely used for various tasks, including misinformation detection [21], claim verification [22], and credibility analysis [23]. However, they have faced criticism for their limitations as described earlier. In addition, they do not capture ambiguous fact-checking scenarios frequently encountered in the real world. Glockner et al. [12] demonstrated that most existing datasets primarily focus on clear-cut cases where evidence either definitively supports or refutes a claim. In contrast, real-world fact-checking often involves incomplete, contradictory, or inconclusive evidence, requiring more nuanced decision-making. This oversimplification hinders the development of automated factchecking systems that can effectively handle complex cases. 

Given these challenges, our work focuses on three key areas where fact-checking datasets are most applicable: (1) automated fact-checking, which involves developing models trained on factchecking reports to verify claims; (2) analysing the fact-checking ecosystem, which examines fact-checking practices, inconsistencies, and trends across different organisations; and (3) credibility assessment, which seeks to evaluate the trustworthiness of factcheckers and their verdicts. We believe that FACTors is well-suited to these tasks, offering a more comprehensive and structured resource for advancing research in these domains. In this section, we summarise key past research work in these three subdomains, providing the context for how FACTors contributes to ongoing research in fact-checking. Table 1 presents a comparative overview of relevant datasets, highlighting their characteristics in relation to FACTors.

Snippet: The automated fact-checking process entails a three-stage pipeline namely claim detection, evidence retrieval and claim-verification. In this section, we discuss limitations of prior datasets and motivate the need for a realistic open-domain setup currently absent in existing datasets. Majority of the existing datasets primarily focus on synthetically curated claims from Wikipedia articles [13,33,2,20,28,24]. Evaluation of automated fact-checking systems on such benchmarks is not representative of real-world claims encountered by fact-checkers motivating the need for curation of such real-world claims. Recent efforts like [15] focus on creating more realistic claims from Wikipedia by identifying cited statements, but fall short and do not reflect the typical distribution of claims verified by fact-checkers as the claims are still synthetic. More recently, substantial effort has been diverted to collection of previously fact-checked real-world claims in politics [3,25,5], science [40,37,43], health [17] and climate [7] domains. However, none of these benchmarks primarily focus on numerical claims, which comprise a substantial portion of real-world claims occurring in political debates or other contexts which comprise numerical quantities. Hence, automated fact-checking systems must account for numerical understanding capabilities that are required for evidence retrieval and claim verification to fact-check such claims. Moreover, existing datasets also do not have a realistic evidence collection due to leakage of manual fact-checker "gold" evidence documents and related verdicts. This leakage may induce the claim verification models to learn shortcuts or overfit to fact-verification justification from manual fact-checkers. Additionally, the data collection pipeline for these benchmarks rely on heuristic search from open web search engines which solely uses the claim as search query. While this may work well for simple synthetic claims, real-world claims are often complex that require multiple aspects to be verified. Hence, using only the original claims as query may limit the evidences collected due to reliance on surface level matches to claim ignoring the numerical and other aspects of the claim. 

More recently, QuanTemp [34] addresses these gaps by curating a realistic open-domain benchmark focusing entirely on numerical claims.

Title: Evaluating Language Models for Biomedical Fact-Checking: A Benchmark Dataset for Cancer Variant Interpretation Verification
Snippet: Most existing fact-checking benchmarks are based on general 31,32 , or political knowledge 33 and are unsuitable for fact-checking in a scientific context. Scientific publications are particularly challenging, as they rely on technical language, jargon, and domain-specific expertise that make it difficult for NLP models to verify claims. Existing scientific fact-checking datasets are further limited by relying primarily on abstracts, overlooking claims that can only be verified using full-text evidence 30,34 . This limitation is critical: in the CIViC knowledgebase, 61% of clinically relevant claims depend on experimental results or tables not present in abstracts. Yet working with the full-text introduces significant challenges to language models, which often struggle with longer inputs 35 . To add to this complexity, precision oncology utilizes numerous domain-specific synonyms, aliases, and nomenclature that evolve with time. No benchmark currently exists for evaluating fact-checking in biomedical knowledgebases, leaving a critical gap at the intersection of AI and precision oncology. 

To address this gap, we present CIViC-Fact, an expert-curated benchmark dataset built to advance automated fact-checking and claim verification in the biomedical domain. CIViC-Fact brings several innovations that make it a powerful resource for evaluating biomedical language models, especially in precision oncology. Unlike most existing science-focused NLP datasets 30,34 , which rely mainly on abstracts, CIViC-Fact includes evidence drawn from the full text of biomedical publications and incorporates both structured and unstructured evidence, such as tabular data and free text, reflecting the heterogeneous formats used in biomedical literature. Claims are written in a structured (tabular) format aligned with the CIViC data model, allowing for precise and interpretable fact-checking. Given the complexity of variant interpretation, annotations in CIViC-Fact were generated by 13 expert annotators from multiple institutions achieving a high level of agreement (77.9%). This high agreement shows that, with sufficient context, experts can reliably judge claim veracity, setting a clear benchmark for models. By incorporating variant interpretations, full-text evidence, and expert-validated gold labels, CIViC-Fact offers a challenging and realistic benchmark for the development and evaluation of trustworthy biomedical language models.
</snippet>

Title: Multi2Claim: Generating Scientific Claims from Multi-Choice Questions for Scientific Fact-Checking
Snippet: Training machine learning models to successfully perform scientific fact-checking tasks is challenging due to the expertise bottleneck that limits the availability of appropriate training datasets. In this task, models use textual evidence to confirm scientific claims, which requires data that contains extensive domain-expert annotation. Consequently, the number of existing scientific-fact-checking datasets and the sizes of those datasets are limited. However, these limitations do not apply to multiple-choice question datasets because of the necessity of domain exams in the modern education system. As one of the first steps towards addressing the fact-checking dataset scarcity problem in scientific domains, we propose a pipeline for automatically converting multiple-choice questions into fact-checking data, which we call Multi2Claim. By applying the proposed pipeline, we generated two large-scale datasets for scientific-fact-checking tasks: Med-Fact and Gsci-Fact for the medical and general science domains, respectively. These two datasets are among the first examples of large-scale scientific-fact-checking datasets. We developed baseline models for the verdict prediction task using each dataset. Additionally, we demonstrated that the datasets could be used to improve performance with respect to the F 1 weighted metric on existing fact-checking datasets such as SciFact, HEALTHVER, COVID-Fact, and CLIMATE-FEVER. In some cases, the improvement in performance was up to a 26% increase.
</snippet>
